notes.b: Inputs are what a family brings into the management process at the start.
points: Human resources are the time, energy, skills and knowledge of family members, which are used to make and carry out decisions.
Material resources are equipment, ingredients, clothing, furniture and other household goods used in the task.
Needs are necessities that must be met, such as food, shelter and warmth.
Wants are desires that go beyond necessities, such as a particular brand, a holiday or a new appliance.
Goals are the outcomes the family sets out to achieve, such as a balanced weekly budget or a family meal on the table by six o'clock.
Inputs are the starting point: a poorly defined need or goal at this stage leads to a result that does not meet the family's needs.

notes.b: Throughputs are the actions a family takes to change its inputs into outputs.
points: Planning: gathering information, identifying the alternatives, weighing them up and deciding on a course of action.
Organising: allocating tasks and responsibilities, deciding who does what and when, and arranging the resources each task needs.
Implementing: putting the plan into action, such as booking, buying, cooking or cleaning.
Adjusting during implementation: changes are made when needs arise, such as an unexpected guest or a shortage of an ingredient.
A plan lists the steps in order and the resources each step needs, so that work can be checked against it.

notes.b: Outputs are the results produced by the throughputs, and they are measured against the goals set in the inputs.
points: Goals achieved: whether the outcome matches the goals the family set.
Changes in values, goals and standards: the result may show that a goal or standard was unrealistic and needs to be revised.
Satisfaction: whether family members are happy with the result and whether their needs and wants were met.
Evaluation: an assessment of whether time, money and energy were used efficiently and effectively.
Effective use of feedback: information about the result is fed back into the system so that the next cycle of planning is improved.

notes.b: A decision is a choice of one course of action from a set of alternatives.
points: Steps in decision-making: identify the problem or need, gather information, list the options, weigh each option against the goals and resources, choose one and act on it.
Review after acting: check whether the decision achieved the goal, and record what should be done differently next time.
Sharing information and ideas before a decision allows the family to allocate tasks fairly.
Decisions made with the views of all members help to resolve conflict and build commitment to the outcome.
Decision-making gives members a broader view of the issues and improves the efficiency of the family's work.
Decisions are easier when the family's values and goals have been agreed beforehand.

notes.b: Communication is the sharing of information, ideas, values and concerns between family members.
points: Communication is needed at every stage: agreeing goals in the inputs, allocating tasks in organising and reporting progress in implementing.
Open discussion of what is and is not working provides the feedback that is used to evaluate the outputs.
Family meetings, a shared written list or a shared calendar are practical ways to communicate decisions.
A decision that is not communicated to every member can lead to duplicated work, missed tasks and conflict.

notes.h: Planning routines for modern patterns of living
points: Modern families may include two working adults, shift workers, lone parents or a parent working from home, and routines must be planned around these patterns.
Work sharing: tasks such as cooking, shopping, laundry and cleaning are divided between members.
Responsibility for family tasks: each member is given a defined task for which they are accountable.
Delegation: an adult passes a task to another member and gives them the instructions and resources needed to complete it.
Gender equity: household tasks are shared on the basis of ability and availability rather than assigned by sex.
Checklists for routines: a daily or weekly checklist lists each task, who completes it and when it is due.
Work schedules: a written timetable, such as a weekly cleaning rota, shows the sequence of tasks and who is responsible for each one.

notes.h: Applying the management framework to a named event (Also examined)
notes.b: The framework can be used for meal planning, money and home management, problem solving and decision-making. A family birthday party is used here as the example.
points: Inputs: the need is a celebration; the goal is a happy party for a child; the want is a particular cake; the human resources are time and help from relatives; the material resources are food, decorations and invitations; the money available sets the budget.
Throughputs: planning the guest list and the budget; organising who buys food, who prepares the room and who sends invitations; implementing the plan and adjusting for extra guests.
Outputs: whether the goal of a happy party was achieved, whether the money was kept within budget, whether members were satisfied, and what would improve the next event.
Feedback from the outputs is recorded so that the next party is planned more efficiently.
Time: allows planning and avoids waste; tasks are completed more efficiently when time is scheduled.
People: family members make and carry out decisions and tasks.
Skills and knowledge: support problem solving, healthy meals and budgeting.
Equipment: saves time and energy; a washing machine, for example, replaces hours of hand washing.
Human energy: allows tasks to be completed in an acceptable and harmonious way.

keyTerms.definition: The model of a management system made up of inputs, throughputs and outputs.
The resources, needs, wants and goals a family brings into the management process.
The planning, organising and implementing actions that change inputs into outputs.
The results of the management process, including goals achieved, satisfaction and evaluation.
Necessities that must be met, such as food, shelter and warmth.
The outcomes a family sets out to achieve.
Passing a task to another member together with the instructions and resources needed to complete it.
Information about the result of an action, used to improve the next cycle of management.
Choosing one course of action from a set of alternatives after weighing them against goals and resources.
The sharing of information, ideas, values and concerns between family members.

factCards.term: Three components of the management process
Five outputs checked at the end of a management cycle
factCards.definition: Goals achieved; changes in values, goals and standards; satisfaction; evaluation; effective use of feedback.
Identify the problem or need; gather information; weigh the alternatives against goals and resources; choose a course of action and review it.

factCards.term: Three benefits of shared decision-making in a family
factCards.definition: It shares information and ideas; it allocates tasks fairly; it helps to resolve conflict.

factCards.term: Four resources, other than money, needed for a good management system
factCards.definition: Time, people (human energy), skills and knowledge, and equipment.

factCards.term: Three ways household tasks can be shared in modern families
factCards.definition: Work sharing, delegation and rotating tasks on the basis of fairness rather than sex.

questions.prompt: Name the three stages of the management process and describe how one of them could be used when planning a family meal.
questions.model: Stages (3 marks): inputs (needs, wants, goals, human and material resources); throughputs (planning, organising, implementing); outputs (goals achieved, satisfaction, evaluation and feedback). Description (3 marks), for example: planning the weekly menu within the food budget, using the family's needs and time; organising who shops and who cooks; implementing by preparing the meal and adjusting for a late arrival; evaluating whether the meal met the family's needs and whether the money was used well.

questions.prompt: Using the management framework, explain how a family could plan and evaluate a family holiday. Refer to decision-making and communication in your answer.
questions.model: Inputs: the need for a break, goals such as rest and family time, wants such as a particular destination, human resources (time, skills, energy of members) and material resources and money that set the budget. Throughputs: planning involves gathering information on costs and options and deciding on a course of action; organising allocates tasks such as booking, packing and arranging transport; implementing carries out the plan and adjusts for changes. Decision-making: identify the options, weigh them against the budget and goals, choose one and review it. Communication: members share information and views so that decisions are agreed and tasks are not duplicated or missed. Outputs: evaluate whether the goals were achieved, whether the budget was kept, whether all members were satisfied and record feedback for planning the next holiday.
